concepts.name: Historical Origins and Patronage of Thanjavur Painting
key_dimensions: Founding period under Nayaka rulers (16th century) vs. peak development under Maratha rulers of Thanjavur (18th–19th century)
Role of the Thanjavur Maratha court, especially Raja Serfoji II, as primary patrons
Influence of earlier Vijayanagara painting traditions as a precursor style
Distinction between court-sponsored works vs. later commercial/temple-based production

concepts.name: Geographical Origin and GI Tag Status
key_dimensions: Specific origin in Thanjavur (Tanjore), Tamil Nadu — not to be confused with other South Indian painting traditions
Geographical Indication (GI) tag granted under the GI of Goods Act, 1999 — year and registration details
Implications of GI tag for artisan protection and commercial rights
Common UPSC trap: distinguishing Thanjavur's GI from other Tamil Nadu GI-tagged crafts (e.g., Kancheepuram silk)

concepts.name: Core Material Technique: Layered Gesso and Embossing
key_dimensions: Use of chalk powder or zinc oxide mixed with adhesive to create raised relief (gesso work) for ornamentation
Application on a wooden base (teak/jackfruit) covered with cloth — the 'cloth-and-paste' base layer
Distinction between the flat painted background and the three-dimensional embossed figures
UPSC trap: Thanjavur uses gesso for relief; do not confuse with the flat wash technique of Mysore painting

concepts.name: Use of Gold Leaf and Semi-Precious Stone Embellishments
key_dimensions: Application of gold foil over gesso relief as a defining characteristic — makes it distinct from most other Indian painting schools
Use of semi-precious stones (rubies, emeralds, diamonds in historical pieces; glass substitutes in contemporary works)
Significance of gold in iconographic/religious context (divinity, opulence of deities)
Comparison with Mysore painting which also uses gold but with thinner application and different base technique

concepts.name: Iconographic Themes and Subject Matter
key_dimensions: Predominantly Hindu devotional themes: Krishna Leela, Dashavatara, Rama, Devi, Ganesha — rooted in Vaishnavite and Shaivite traditions
Influence of Bhagavata Purana as the primary textual source for narrative compositions
Occasional Christian and Jain themes produced during colonial period for diverse patrons
UPSC trap: unlike folk arts such as Madhubani (nature/fertility themes), Thanjavur is almost exclusively temple-deity-centric

concepts.name: Stylistic Features: Composition and Aesthetics
key_dimensions: Frontal, static, hieratic depiction of deities — figures are rigid and symmetrical, not dynamic
Flat, unmodeled background (typically red or green) with no landscape or perspective
Large, prominent eyes; full rounded faces; elaborate ornamentation as aesthetic hallmarks
Comparison trap: Kalamkari (narrative, elongated figures) vs. Thanjavur (static, frontal, jewel-encrusted)

concepts.name: Pigments and Color Palette: Traditional vs. Contemporary
key_dimensions: Traditional use of vegetable and mineral pigments: lapis lazuli for blue, vermillion for red, lamp black, etc.
Shift to chemical/synthetic colors in modern production — impact on authenticity and GI compliance
Specific dominant colors: deep reds, greens, blues with gold as overarching visual element
Relevance to sustainability and revival debates — Ministry of Textiles and Handicrafts Board initiatives

concepts.name: Base Material and Substrate Evolution
key_dimensions: Traditional base: wooden plank (teak or jackfruit wood) overlaid with cloth treated with chalk paste
Modern adaptations using hardboard, cardboard, or canvas — and the controversy over authenticity
The multi-layered preparation process: wood → cloth → chalk-gum paste → painting surface
UPSC angle: process-based questions often ask about the sequence or unique material not found in other schools

concepts.name: Comparison with Mysore Painting: Key Distinctions
key_dimensions: Both use gold leaf and devotional themes — the most common UPSC confusion point
Mysore: thinner gold application (gold leaf on lac/gum), Karnataka origin, Wodeyar patronage, more delicate lines
Thanjavur: thick gesso embossing, heavier gold foil, Tamil Nadu origin, Maratha patronage, bolder composition
Both are distinct from Mughal miniatures in subject matter and technique — triangular comparison possible

concepts.name: Artisan Community and Hereditary Craft Transmission
key_dimensions: Traditionally practiced by the 'Raju' community (Kshatriya painters) and later by 'Devanga' weavers-turned-painters
Hereditary transmission within families — guru-shishya and family lineage models
Impact of declining patronage post-independence and shift to tourist/commercial market
Government schemes: Shilp Guru award, National Awards by Ministry of Textiles for master artisans

concepts.name: Thanjavur Painting vs. Tanjore Glass Painting
key_dimensions: Tanjore glass painting is a separate tradition on glass surface — distinct from the wooden-base Thanjavur painting
Glass painting influenced by European reverse-glass painting techniques introduced during colonial period
Both originate from the same region but are classified differently in craft taxonomy
UPSC trap: questions may conflate the two; key differentiator is the substrate (wood+cloth vs. glass)

concepts.name: Role of Temples and Religious Function
key_dimensions: Paintings traditionally used as portable icons for home shrines and gifted during religious ceremonies
Strong connection to Vaishnava temple culture of the Kaveri delta region (Srirangam, Kumbakonam)
Used as 'utsava' or festive gifts — not purely decorative but ritually significant
Distinction: unlike cave murals or temple frescoes (immovable), Thanjavur paintings are mobile devotional objects

concepts.name: Influence of Maratha Cultural Synthesis
key_dimensions: Thanjavur Marathas (Bhonsle rulers, 1674–1855) brought North Indian/Deccan aesthetic sensibilities to Tamil traditions
Fusion of Dravidian iconography with Maratha court aesthetics — visible in costume and ornamentation styles
Raja Serfoji II's role in documenting and institutionalizing the art form at Saraswathi Mahal Library
Cultural synthesis angle: relevant for questions on composite culture and cross-regional artistic exchanges

concepts.name: Contemporary Revival and Institutional Support
key_dimensions: Role of Crafts Council of India and Tamil Nadu Handicrafts Development Corporation (TNHDC) in revival
UNESCO's engagement — not a UNESCO-inscribed art form yet (important 'not' fact for UPSC)
Digital documentation and e-commerce platforms enabling artisan livelihood — TRIFED, Amul-style cooperative models
National Handicrafts and Handlooms Museum (Crafts Museum, New Delhi) — houses significant Thanjavur collections

concepts.name: Thanjavur Painting and the Broader Deccan-South Indian Painting Continuum
key_dimensions: Position within the broader South Indian painting schools: Vijayanagara → Nayaka → Thanjavur continuum
Relationship with Lepakshi murals (Vijayanagara) as stylistic ancestor — shared iconographic vocabulary
Distinct from contemporaneous Kalighat (Bengal), Phad (Rajasthan), and Pattachitra (Odisha) in technique and patronage
UPSC frequently tests ability to place art forms on a chronological and regional matrix

concepts.name: Process Stages: Step-by-Step Production Methodology
key_dimensions: Stage 1: Sketching the outline on the cloth-covered wooden base
Stage 2: Applying gesso paste for raised ornamentation and allowing it to dry
Stage 3: Fixing gold foil and semi-precious stones over gesso areas
Stage 4: Painting the flat areas with pigments and varnishing — sequence is a frequent MCQ target

concepts.name: Export, Economic Significance, and IPR Challenges
key_dimensions: Major export destinations: USA, Europe, Southeast Asia — part of India's handicraft export basket
Threat from cheap imitations produced outside Thanjavur (especially from Andhra Pradesh and China)
GI tag as a legal tool to combat counterfeiting — enforcement mechanisms under GI Act
Role of APEDA and Export Promotion Council for Handicrafts (EPCH) in promoting authentic Thanjavur works

concepts.name: Distinction from Other Tamil Nadu Art Forms
key_dimensions: Thanjavur painting vs. Tanjore Doll (Thanjavur Bommai) — both from same region but entirely different mediums
Difference from Tamil Nadu's Kolam (floor art) and Kalamkari practiced in Tamil Nadu variant
Thanjavur as 'classical' vs. Kolam as 'folk' — hierarchical classification within Indian art traditions
UPSC trap: all Tamil Nadu GI arts are not Thanjavur paintings — Kancheepuram silk, Nilgiris tea, Thanjavur painting are separate GI entries

concepts.name: Philosophical and Aesthetic Underpinnings: Bhakti Movement Influence
key_dimensions: Deep roots in the Bhakti movement — especially Alvar saints' Vaishnavism and Nayanmars' Shaivism
Purpose of art as 'darshan' (auspicious viewing) rather than mere decoration — theological significance of the gaze of the deity
Connection to Nataraja iconography of Chidambaram and Krishna iconography of Guruvayur
Broader UPSC linkage: Bhakti movement's role in shaping regional art, architecture, and literature across India
